old_title: France wildfires latest: Temperatures to reach 44C today as thousands more evacuated
new_title: I joined the fight against France's wildfires. What I witnessed was extraordinary
old_text:
France has warned that the latest intense heatwave hitting the country will peak today, as more towns near Bordeaux were evacuated in the face of raging wildfires.
Temperatures could reach up to 44C in some parts, according to Meteo France, while forecasters in Spain said the heatwave there is expected to continue until Sunday.
French authorities have ordered 4,000 more people to leave tourist sites along the country's Atlantic coast, expanding what may be France's largest peacetime evacuation as a vast wildfire west of Bordeaux raged.
The Gironde fire has burned an area four times the size of Paris and forced 220,000 people to leave their homes.
A renewed heatwave was threatening firefighters' fragile hold on the blaze, and fresh flames have erupted near Grand Crohot, a popular Atlantic beach on the Lège-Cap-Ferret peninsula, local authorities said.
President Emmanuel Macron said France was facing its most difficult situation since the Second World War, urging fire crews to "stay strong".
Spanish authorities say more than 63,000 people have been evacuated from their homes near Madrid.
Gironde fire created black thundercloud in a first for France
At its most violent, the Gironde blaze created a gargantuan black thundercloud, electrified and lit from within.
It generated lightning, violent winds and new fires beyond the original front.
The phenomenon, known as a pyrocumulonimbus cloud, was the first recorded in France.
Heatwave threatens to reignite France's mega-fire near Bordeaux
The heatwave and forecast winds could hamper progress against the blaze that has forced 220,000 people from their homes, authorities for the Gironde region around Bordeaux said.
In a Wednesday morning update on the huge firefighting effort, Gironde authorities said the situation overnight had been "calm" and that the blaze hadn't spread - although it's still not contained a week after it started.
The onset of heatwave temperatures and winds heightened the risk of flames flaring again.
On Tuesday, Gironde authorities ordered 4,000 more people evacuated from tourist sites along the Atlantic coast, widening what may be France's largest peacetime evacuation.
"The situation remains complicated. That's clear. We're not out of the woods," Gironde prefect Sophie Brocas said Tuesday evening.
But she also gave the go-ahead for 60,000 evacuees to return to their homes in three Bordeaux suburbs that haven't burned.
Watch: Firefighter's helmet camera captures battle against France's raging wildfires
Mapped: The areas in France and Spain affected by raging wildfires
More than 360,000 people have been forced to evacuate their homes as wildfires continue to rage across Spain and France.
At least one man has been killed in Spain and dozens of others have been injured, including at least 68 firefighters in France.
Government officials from both countries have commented on the historic nature of the blaze, with Madrid's regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso describing it as "the worst fire in the history of the region".
Below we look at the areas affected and evacuated as a result of the wildfires.
France heatwave to peak today
France has warned that the latest intense heatwave hitting the country will peak today, as more towns near Bordeaux were evacuated in the face of raging wildfires.
Temperatures could reach up to 44C in some parts, according to Meteo France, while forecasters in Spain said the heatwave there is expected to continue until Sunday.
French authorities have ordered 4,000 more people to leave tourist sites along the country's Atlantic coast, expanding what may be France's largest peacetime evacuation as a vast wildfire west of Bordeaux raged.
The air is unbreathable, say people forced to flee homes in Bordeaux
People caught up in the wildfires inching towards Bordeaux have described how they are struggling to breathe as smoke from the fires has forced them to flee their homes.
More than 200,000 people have been told to evacuate the area as firefighters battle in a race against time to contain the blaze, which burns within nine miles of the main metropolitan area.
Wildfire response must evolve to keep pace with climate change, EU says
The European Union's response to wildfires needs more funding, greater focus on forest management and enhanced education about fire risk as the climate changes, the head of the bloc's crisis response said, as France and Spain battle deadly blazes.
Wildfires have forced unprecedented evacuations of tens of thousands of people across France and Spain, and torn through a region already battered by a blisteringly hot and dry summer.
"Climate change is accelerating. So our response must evolve just as quickly," Hadja Lahbib, the EU's Crisis Management Commissioner, told Reuters.
"We must prepare for risks before disasters strike, and not simply react afterwards."
Lahbib said it was not enough to just purchase more firefighting equipment, and that countries should also be investing more of their EU funding in forest management practices that reduce wildfire risk, and should better educate citizens on "what behaviour they absolutely must avoid", to reduce fire risk. Around 90 per cent of wildfires are started by human activities, such as campfires or discarded cigarettes.
Firefighters say they've never seen anything like Spain's record blazes
Spanish firefighter Javier García has never faced anything like the record blaze raging near Madrid in his two decades protecting woodlands and rural communities.
"This doesn't have a precedent," he said.
Spanish prime minister says 'end of the tunnel' is near
Prime minister Pedro Sánchez said on Tuesday that Spain is beginning to see "light at the end of the tunnel" in its battle against the wildfires, although some fires continue raging and he warned the next few hours remain crucial.
Authorities allowed most people in the central Toledo province to return to their homes, lifting a state of emergency introduced on 23 July. Fires still raged in the Madrid region nearby.
"We are starting to see the end of the tunnel in the fight against these fires," Mr Sanchez told reporters.
Black thundercloud creates own lightning, wind and new blazes
At its most violent, the Gironde blaze created a gargantuan black thundercloud, electrified and lit from within. It generated lightning, violent winds and new fires beyond the original front.
The phenomenon, known as a pyrocumulonimbus cloud, was the first recorded in France.
France's national weather service placed Gironde under a yellow heat warning, forecasting inland temperatures of 33 to 35C.
new_text:
The pick-up truck shudders to a halt and an outstretched arm signals the silhouette of a lone deer racing through the blackened woods.
There are six of us squeezed into the back of the Toyota Hilux, all clinging onto a caged water tank as we bounce along the dirt roads of a forest ravaged by wildfires. Sandy firebreaks have created a stark contrast between the verdant woodland surrounding Lacanau and the devastated areas in monochrome, still heavy with smoke.
Lacanau, a coastal town some 30 miles west of Bordeaux, has mobilised over the past week to meet the fire threat head on. Dozens of volunteers - some as young as 18 - are now working around the clock to guide firefighters, feed the displaced and to put out fires.
I arrived in the commune as visitors were ordered to leave, with a looming heatwave expected to exacerbate the situation in the coming days.
Taxis and buses refused to go directly to the town, and Google regularly showed there was no viable route to Lacanau at all.
Police had set up checkpoints around the perimeter and there was a steady stream of motorhomes coming the other way as we tried to press in.
My guide was Pao Borecka, a 31-year-old who had moved to the woodland commune six years ago and started organising cultural events and painting.
Now, she says, she has no time to paint while running between the canal at Pont du Hourbiel - where volunteers are pumping water and running patrols - and the town, where locals are preparing food and tending to evacuees.
Residents have been playing their part for nearly a week since the wildfires broke out on 22 July, razing hundreds of buildings and forcing nearly a quarter of a million people in the wider area from their homes.
The fires have drawn in emergency services from across the country, but they seem to depend on the bravery of the locals, willing to risk their lives to show them through the woods. Every few minutes, a patrol car arrives back at the canal and another heads off laden with volunteers, sometimes in front of fire trucks.
After several days in the forest, some of the volunteers have eyes reddened and voices broken from the smoke. The long walks into the woods have left others with burns on their ankles and blisters upon blisters on their feet. Pao says she has lost two pairs of shoes already walking through the smouldering forests, which warm your feet if you stand too long. The job is hard, but it has to be done.
The visit itself is bleak; the air is thick and poisonous, refugees rest on camp beds in an empty hall, and people speak candidly of plans to flee the commune and rescue loved ones if the fire worsens. But it is the fundamental good-heartedness of the people of Lacanau that shines through.
All expect to be here until the fire is out. None hesitate or falter in giving all they have to the gargantuan effort ahead of them. Some say they have been here for five days already, some working 15 hours a day, but nobody for a moment seems to lose sight of their task.
Many have lost businesses and had to take in friends, relatives and strangers displaced by the fires. But they also know how much they still have to lose; in Le Porge - half an hour south - it is said more than 150 homes have been gutted since last week.
And so, despite the tiredness, despite the sun and the mental strain that everybody acknowledges, columns of volunteers continue to march from the canal to the forest "like ants", with watering cans and buckets to stop ashes from reigniting.
In the town, people do the same. Grandparents make sandwiches for delivery to the volunteers. Local restaurants, closed by the fires, offer what they can. Pick-up trucks stream back and forth with water and aid while Canadair water bombers swoop overhead, the frontlines now just two kilometres away.
And even as an outsider, the locals ensure I am safe: they offer me a face mask before fixing their own; they encourage me to eat when we are tired from carrying water; they call through a list of taxi companies to find one willing to drive me back out while they remain.
I am in awe of Pao and her unwavering energy for doing what is right. She acknowledges the risk to herself by continuing her work, and recognises when she needs to rest or laugh, to self-regulate. But she and her neighbours move with an infectious sense of duty to keep going in spite of all that has been lost.
We see on our journey from the back of the pickup truck spreads of animal feed and water left out in the charred forests for the other lives touched by the fires. This job, like that, demands at times a calm detachment to carry on without being overwhelmed by emotion. But at others, it is impossible not to be moved by the gentle reminders, in the worst of times, of the prevailing good in humanity.
